grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: How Celan moves through action, questions, commands, negation, and conditions.
grammar_guide.csv.guideSections: [{"title":"The Core Idea: Action Comes First","body":"In Celan, what is happening is always more important than who is doing it. The language focuses on the event itself. When you speak Celan, you are not just an individual forcing your will on the world; you are a participant in a larger action."},{"title":"Default Word Order: Verb-Subject-Object (VSO)","body":"Because the action is the most important part of the story, a standard Celan sentence begins with the Verb, then the Subject, and finally the Object or destination.","list":["English: I go to the water. (Actor -> Action -> Target)","Celan: `Go I to the water.` (Action -> Actor -> Target)"]},{"title":"Forming Questions and Commands","body":"Celan keeps sentence-shaping simple. Instead of relying on tone or heavy rearrangement, it places a small signpost word at the very beginning of the sentence to announce its shape.","list":["Questions: place `ra` at the start of the sentence to make it a question.","Commands: place `va` at the start of the sentence to give an instruction or command."]},{"title":"Negation (Saying \"No\" or \"Not\")","body":"To make a sentence negative, place `ver` directly in front of the verb. In a negative question, `ver` slides between the question signpost `ra` and the verb."},{"title":"Conditionals (\"If\" sentences)","body":"To say if, place `rath` at the beginning of the sentence. This tells the listener that the action is conditional or hypothetical."},{"title":"What to Notice","body":null,"list":[{"title":"The action arrives before the actor","copy":"Because the verb comes first, your listener knows what is happening before they know who is involved."},{"title":"Signposts are structural","copy":"Words like `ra` and `va` are not decorative. They sit at the front of the sentence to frame what is about to happen before the action even arrives."},{"title":"The lowercase rule still applies","copy":"Sentences begin with lowercase unless the first word is a name, a grand concept, or the pronoun `I`. Because of this, signposts like `ra`, `va`, `rath`, and `ver` will usually be lowercase."}]}]

Command: `va var dren!` (Go to the water!)

grammar_guide.csv.rule_name: Word Building: How Celan Grows Words
grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How roots, compounds, suffixes, and sound-shaping grow Celan words from core ideas.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: How roots, compounds, suffixes, and sound-shaping grow Celan words from core ideas.
grammar_guide.csv.guideSections: [{"title":"The Core Idea: Roots as Seeds","body":"In Celan, words are not random strings of letters. The language is built like a set of blocks. Many Celan words grow from roots, the core ideas used to build related forms. Think of a root as the seed of the meaning. For example, `Krez` means Fire or Heat, and `Dren` means Water. Every word you build from these seeds carries a piece of that original meaning."},{"title":"Compounding (Smashing Ideas Together)","body":"To make a new concept, roots can combine into one word. The order matters because it affects the meaning; check the established form before using a new combination.","list":["Important Rule: We do not use hyphens to fuse roots together. They are completely merged.","Example: `Morl` (Mountain) + `Dren` (Water) seamlessly becomes `Morldren` (Waterfall).","Example: `Bel` (Binding / weaving) + `Shara` (Path / journey) becomes `Belshara` (woven path / structured journey)."]},{"title":"Derivation (Adding Suffixes and Prefixes)","body":"You can attach small grammatical tags to a root to change how the word behaves.","list":["Making Verbs: Add the suffix `-aen` to turn a noun into an action. `Dren` (Water) becomes `drenaen` (To drink).","Time Travel (Tense): While English uses separate words like will or did, Celan builds time directly onto the verb using a hyphen. Add `nor-` for the future or `tha-` for the past. `var` (go) becomes `nor-var` (will go)."]},{"title":"Pluralization (Making Things Plural)","body":"Making a word plural in Celan is incredibly simple. If the word ends in a consonant, add `-in`. If it ends in a vowel, add `-n`.","list":["Example: `Ser` (Friend) becomes `serin` (Friends).","If a noun already ends in a vowel, the plural stays light: you simply add `-n`."]},{"title":"The Magic of `-eth`","body":"This is one of the most important suffixes in the language. Adding `-eth` to a word means having the quality of or the essence of. It is the easiest way to turn a noun into a descriptive adjective.","list":["Example: `Kal` (Strength) becomes `kaleth` (Strong).","Example: `Wor` (Abundance) becomes `woreth` (Full / abundant)."]},{"title":"What to Notice","body":null,"list":[{"title":"Valid builds vs. canon","copy":"Roots can suggest a possible new word, but a possible build is not automatically an established dictionary word."},{"title":"Sound smoothing (Euphony)","copy":"Some speakers insert a vowel to ease a difficult consonant cluster. A smoother form can coexist with an unsmoothed form; smoothing is not required for every word."},{"title":"Culture shapes the word","copy":"Cultural voices may prefer different sounds and word choices. Treat the forms below as illustrations of that choice, not automatic new headwords."}]}]

grammar_guide.csv.rule_name: Number and Measure: How Celan Counts the World
grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan builds numbers, expresses quantity, and uses measures.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: How Celan builds numbers, expresses quantity, and uses measures.
grammar_guide.csv.guideSections: [{"title":"Base Numbers (0–10)","body":"In Celan, you only need to memorize eleven core numbers. Every other number in the entire language is built from these basic seeds.","list":["0 = `verin`","1 = `unar`","2 = `del`","3 = `tren`","4 = `quen`","5 = `peth`","6 = `senar`","7 = `sethe`","8 = `oven`","9 = `nevar`","10 = `tenar`"]},{"title":"Scaling Prefixes (Growing the Numbers)","body":"Instead of learning entirely new words for twenty, thirty, or a hundred, Celan attaches a scale marker to the front of a base number.","list":["Tens: add `Ten-` (for example, `Ten-del` = 20, literally Two tens).","Hundreds: add `Hek-` (for example, `Hek-quen` = 400).","Thousands: add `Mel-` (for example, `Mel-unar` = 1,000).","Tens of Thousands: add `Fen-` (for example, `Fen-peth` = 50,000)."]},{"title":"Building Larger Numbers (Stacking)","body":"To make a larger, complex number, you stack the blocks from largest to smallest. The language naturally treats this as addition.","list":["Example: `tenar unar` = 11, built by placing 10 and 1 next to each other.","Example: `Ten-del peth` = 25, built by stating twenty and then five."]},{"title":"Simple Arithmetic","body":"Addition is invisible. It happens naturally just by stating the numbers together in order. To subtract, use the specific word `Ven` (minus). It acts as a structural wall between the two numbers."},{"title":"Measuring with Shen","body":"`shen` can name a unit of quantity. Put the number before the measure word, as in the established pattern `peth shen` (“five measures”). A measure is different from coinage, another meaning of `shen`."},{"title":"Quantification and Articles","body":"Celan does not waste breath on small, empty words. There are no direct translations for the English words a or the. If you say `dren`, the listener understands from context whether you mean water or the water. When you need to describe quantity without an exact number, place a quantifier right before the noun.","list":["`ilinor` = all","`melen` = many","`som` = some / a few","`felin` = few","`ekor` = each / every"]},{"title":"What to Notice","body":null,"list":[{"title":"Numbers are built, not just memorized","copy":"Once you learn 0–10 and the four scaling prefixes, you can mathematically construct any number you need."},{"title":"Scale markers matter","copy":"The tiny prefix you choose completely changes the size of your statement. `unar` is one, but `Mel-unar` becomes a thousand."},{"title":"Subtraction has visible logic","copy":"Addition is as simple as placing number blocks together, but subtraction requires the explicit marker `Ven` so the listener knows something is being taken away."}]}]

grammar_guide.csv.rule_name: Gender, Address, and Social Use: How Celan Connects People
grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan handles identity, respect, address, and social nuance through form choice.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: How Celan handles identity, respect, address, and social nuance through form choice.
grammar_guide.csv.guideSections: [{"title":"The Core Idea: Identity is an Essence, Not a Box","body":"In Celan, who you are is not a rigid, unchanging label assigned at birth. Identity is based on your essence and the qualities you embody right now. Because the Ohnoshan worldview values flow and change, identity is seen as a journey (`Shara`); the word you use to describe yourself may evolve as you grow older or change your path in life."},{"title":"Gender Terms (The Seeds of Identity)","body":"Instead of relying only on strict biological labels, Celan uses three core seeds of essence to describe people.","list":["`Kadren`: Masculine essence (strength, groundedness).","`Azan`: Feminine essence (nurturing, fluidity).","`Thee`: Neutral essence (balance, unity).","From these seeds come standard terms like `Kadron` (man), `Azron` (woman), and `Theon` (neutral person).","Because identity is fluid, you can also mix these roots. A man who embodies feminine, nurturing qualities is an `Azon`, and a woman who embodies fierce, masculine traits is a `Kadon`."]},{"title":"Combining Qualities and Poetic Expressions","body":"Celan encourages you to layer these terms to capture human nuance. You can combine forms to describe someone as a `Kadron-Azon`, a man with both masculine and feminine qualities. These terms can also be used poetically to describe how someone interacts with the world, such as a neutral person who brings balance to a situation.","list":["Example: `Kadron-Azon` marks a man carrying both masculine and feminine qualities.","Example: `Theon` can be used poetically for someone whose presence brings balance into a tense situation."]},{"title":"Politeness and Address Forms (Showing Respect)","body":"In English, we often show respect through tone of voice. In Celan, respect is built directly into the words themselves by adding honorific tags and choosing elevated titles.","list":["The Respect Tag (`Li-`): attach this to the front of a name or title to show polite respect to a stranger or elder. Example: `Li-Ser` = Respected friend.","The High Honor Tag (`-en`): attach this to the end of a title for immense, formal reverence. Example: `Liorinen` = Honored Elder.","Specific respectful titles also exist, such as `Liana` (Lady), `Lianor` (Sir), or `Seren` (Guardian)."]},{"title":"Cultural Variation (Reading the Room)","body":"Different nations and situations require different levels of formality. A speaker's choice of words tells you immediately how they view the social dynamic.","list":["Formal vs. Casual: in a royal court or sacred temple, you use elevated words like `aen` (to speak) and `var` (to purposefully go). In a marketplace or among friends, you might use casual words like `kel` (to chat) and `min` (to wander or head over).","Regional Flavors: the oceanic people of Pelagae value fluidity and may use `Azon` frequently for their spiritual men. The mountain warriors of Valkeldor value strength and may favor `Kadon` to honor their warrior women."]},{"title":"What to Notice","body":null,"list":[{"title":"Celan does social work through form choice","copy":"Adding a tiny sound like `Li-` immediately changes the social boundary between two speakers."},{"title":"Respect is not a tiny side feature","copy":"It is architectural. If you want to be polite, you cannot just smile; you must actually construct your words differently."},{"title":"Some forms are literal, some relational, some culturally charged","copy":"Calling someone a `Theon` may be a literal description of their identity, but in some places it can also be a culturally charged compliment honoring balance."}]}]

Follow the spelling shown for each word; capitals are not freely added just to show emotion."},{"title":"The Sentence-Initial Lowercase Rule","body":"An ordinary sentence can start with a lowercase verb or a marker such as `ra`. Names and established capitalized forms keep their capitals wherever they appear."},{"title":"The Sanctity of `I`","body":"The first-person singular pronoun is written `I`. The app also writes the second-person pronoun `Ya` with a capital letter. Follow the established spelling of each pronoun rather than a rule that only `I` may be capitalized.","list":["`var I an dren.` — I go to the water.","`ra var Ya?` — Where do you go?"]},{"title":"Names, Titles, and Sacred Concepts","body":"When do you capitalize words? grammar_guide.csv.rule_name: Cultural Voice: How Ohnosha Speaks Celan Differently
grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How one universal language develops distinct national voices without breaking into separate dialects.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: How one universal tongue takes on different national voices across Ohnosha.
grammar_guide.csv.guideSections: [{"title":"The Core Idea: One Language, Many Voices","body":"While Celan is the universal tongue of Ohnosha, its application across the world is not monolithic. Generations of local use have given rise to distinct Cultural Voices or National Vernaculars. These are not separate dialects with different grammar rules. They are different habits of vocabulary choice, metaphor, sentence texture, and phonetic preference."},{"title":"What Changes from Culture to Culture","body":"Cultural Voice appears in word choice, metaphor, sentence feel, and especially in how a people applies the Rule of Euphony. Some cultures smooth words into flowing musical forms. Others deliberately keep harsh consonant clusters to sound practical, martial, or severe."},{"title":"The Eight National Vernaculars","body":null,"list":[{"title":"Verdalrisian (Poetic & Harmonious)","copy":"Deeply connected to the living forests, the Verdalrisian voice is lyrical, patient, and rich with natural metaphor. Because beauty in speech matters deeply to them, they are the most likely to use advanced vowel harmony and highly smoothed forms."},{"title":"Pelagaean (Fluid & Melodic)","copy":"Reflecting their oceanic origins, Pelagaean speech is fluid, communal, and poetic. Their vernacular is saturated with metaphors of water, tides, and flow. Like the Verdalrisians, they heavily prefer smoothed, euphonic pronunciations."},{"title":"Zarithan (Pragmatic & Guttural)","copy":"Shaped by barren deserts and a nomadic survivalist spirit, the Zarithan voice is practical and direct. They value clarity and efficiency above all else, and often break euphonic expectations to preserve harsh consonant clusters such as `Krezthal` instead of `Krezathal`."},{"title":"Valkeldorian (Conservative & Harsh)","copy":"Grounded in stone, mountains, and resilience, Valkeldorian language is strong and resolute. Like the Zarithans, they often prefer harder, non-euphonic forms to reflect martial strength and unyielding endurance."},{"title":"Mechuman (Systematic & Standardized)","copy":"Reflecting a society built on technology, magic, and ordered systems, Mechumans value efficiency, logic, and purpose. In speech, they apply Celan phonetic and grammatical rules with exact, systematic consistency."},{"title":"Nivveilian (Patient & Minimalist)","copy":"Shaped by the icy north, Nivveilians are reserved, patient, and stoic. Their vernacular is understated and highly economical, making every sound count."},{"title":"Jasaran (Balanced & Elegant)","copy":"As oasis dwellers, Jasarans blend Zarithan practicality with water-centered mysticism. Their speech seeks careful balance and often aims for a poised, elegant phonetic equilibrium."},{"title":"Marakorian (Formal & Archaic)","copy":"Marakorian speech values discipline, order, refinement, and reverence for tradition. Their Cultural Voice is highly formal and often leans into older, more archaic forms."}]},{"title":"Cultural Voice in Practice","body":"These are not separate grammars. They are different ways of inhabiting the same language. The clearest way to feel the shift is to hear each nation ask or frame something in its own voice. For consistency, the examples below follow the writing conventions used elsewhere in this guide.","list":[{"title":"Verdalrisian","copy":"`lorin shara Ya an Kinnmor, Li-Ser?` — “Where does your path guide you this morning, Respected-Friend?” Listen for the lyrical phrasing, the guided-path imagery, and the patient tone."},{"title":"Pelagaean","copy":"`ra shalil Ya, Ser?` — “Where do you flow, Friend?” Listen for how movement becomes water-language instead of blunt travel-language."},{"title":"Zarithan","copy":"`ra min Ya, Ser?` — “Where are you headed, Friend?” Listen for the directness: fewer flourishes, less metaphor, more survival-minded clarity."},{"title":"Valkeldorian","copy":"`aen shara-ya, Ser!` — “State your path, Friend!” Listen for the command-like firmness and strong, disciplined tone."},{"title":"Mechuman","copy":"`aen Ya varash, Ser.` — “State your destination, Friend.” Listen for the precision: clear, exact, and almost procedural in its phrasing."},{"title":"Nivveilian","copy":"`an eshreth, ra var Ya, Ser?` — “In this hazy sky, where are you going, Friend?” Listen for the spare, quiet atmosphere and restrained emotional temperature."},{"title":"Jasaran","copy":"`shal lorin shara-ya an nor-ka, Ser?` — “Does the light guide your path in this moment, Friend?” Listen for the balance of practicality and mysticism."},{"title":"Marakorian","copy":"`ra rinaen shara-ya lian, Li-Ser?` — “Is your path a proper one, Respected-Friend?” Listen for the formal, judging, order-conscious register."}]},{"title":"What to Notice","body":null,"list":[{"title":"These are voices, not dialects","copy":"The underlying language remains Celan. What changes is how a people inhabits it."},{"title":"Euphony is one of the clearest markers","copy":"A listener can often hear cultural alignment immediately in the choice between a harsh cluster and a smoothed form."},{"title":"Vocabulary and metaphor matter too","copy":"Cultural Voice is not only about sound. It also lives in the metaphors, titles, and preferred registers a people reaches for."}]}]

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: Clear vowel anchors with accepted sound choices for W, X, TH, and AE.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: Celan keeps its single vowels clear. W, X, TH, and AE have accepted alternative sounds; AI has one stable diphthong, and OA has two accepted readings. A word page shows one valid reading, not the only permitted reading.
grammar_guide.csv.guideSections: [{"title":"The core idea","body":"Pronounce Celan clearly without swallowing syllables. A word page gives one useful reading. The alternatives below are also correct and may vary with dialect, pace, emphasis, or performance."},{"title":"W: flowing W or firm V","body":"W may sound like English w, or like a firm v with the teeth against the lower lip. The firm reading is common in northern or martial accents and for sharp emphasis.","list":["`Wek`: wehk or vehk","`Wel`: wehl or vehl","`Worvenak`: wohr-veh-nahk or vor-veh-nahk"]},{"title":"X: KH or KS anywhere","body":"X may be a breathy throat sound, written KH here, or a crisp KS. Either reading can occur at the beginning or inside a word.","list":["`Xar`: khar or ksar","`Xaresh`: khar-esh or ksar-esh","`Xilvar`: kheel-var; `Xilbren`: kseel-brehn","`Dralxar`: dral-khar or dral-ksar"]},{"title":"TH: flowing or sharply aspirated","body":"Flowing TH may be voiceless as in English think or voiced as in this. The sharper reading is T followed by a clear puff of H: t-ha.","list":["`Thar`: thahr or t-hahr","`Thal`: thahl or t-hahl"]},{"title":"AE: three accepted readings","body":"The letters ae may have two beats (ah-eh), one smooth beat (ay as in day), or a bright beat (eye as in sky). Slow ceremonial speech often uses two beats; fast speech or songs may use either one-beat form.","list":["`Aen`: ah-ehn or ayn; the eye reading is also valid","`Rinaen`: ree-nah-ehn or ree-nayn","`Vael`: vah-ehl or vayl"]},{"title":"AI and OA","body":"AI always sounds like eye across registers. OA may sound like oh-ah or wah, depending on speaking speed.","list":["`Aiv`: eyev; `Rinaen-ai`: ree-nayn-eye","`Doa`: doh-ah or dwah"]},{"title":"The five single vowels","body":"Single vowels stay open and clear in the Italian or Spanish style.","list":["`A` = ah as in father; `Terra`: tehr-rah","`E` = eh as in bed; `Dren`: drehn","`I` = ee as in machine; `Ilin`: ee-leen","`O` = oh as in go; `Morl`: mohrl","`U` = oo as in flu; `Zun`: zoon"]},{"title":"SH, ZH, KH, and J","body":"SH sounds as in shine. ZH sounds like the middle sound in measure. KH is a rough sound at the back of the throat. J has the soft ZH sound.","list":["`Shal`: shahl; `Shara`: shah-rah","`Zhir`: zheer; `Zhael`: zhah-ehl (the two-beat AE reading)","`Khumlor`: khoom-lor","`Joreth`: zhor-eth"]},{"title":"MB, ND, and NK at the start","body":"Hum the nasal sound briefly before releasing the next consonant.","list":["`Mbalan`: m-bah-lahn","`Ndem`: n-dehm","`Nkuvath`: n-koo-vahth"]},{"title":"Other consonants","body":"B, D, G, V, and Z are voiced and firm. K, T, and P are clean stops. L and R flow; R may be lightly tapped or rolled. M and N are clear nasal sounds."},{"title":"The Rule of Euphony (Sound-Smoothing)","body":"When fused roots create a harsh or clumsy consonant cluster, a Celan speaker may choose a smoothing vowel to maintain rhythmic flow. The unsmoothed construction remains valid. The neutral choice is often a, while e or o may appear through vowel harmony; before Wek, an euphonic choice uses e or o rather than a.","list":[{"title":"Strong Smoothing Choice","copy":"Harsh, repetitive, or dissonant clusters are the most likely to be smoothed, but smoothing is not grammatically mandatory. Examples include `Morl` + `Thar` -> `Morlathar`, `Rath` + `Thar` -> `Rathathar`, and `Vok` + `Thal` -> `Vokathar`."},{"title":"Stylistic and National Contrast","copy":"For clunky but pronounceable clusters, smoothing becomes a cultural choice. A pragmatic Zarithan or Valkeldorian may prefer `Krezthal` or `Belshara`, while a poetic Pelagaean or Verdalrisian may prefer `Krezathal` or `Belashara`."},{"title":"Forms Normally Left Unsmoothed","copy":"Naturally smooth clusters need no euphonic option, and ancient phonetic fossils normally remain unchanged. Smooth: `Kalvok`, `Kalrath`, `Rethlian`. Fossils: `Belthal`, `Rethvok`."},{"title":"Euphony Before Wek","copy":"When `Wek` is the second root, the euphonic choices are `-ewek` and `-owek`, not `-awek`. This keeps the independent root `Awek` (water spring) distinct. Examples: `Belwek` / `Belewek` / `Belowek`; `Kalwek` / `Kalewek` / `Kalowek`; chosen headword `Mahrowek`, with unsmoothed `Mahrwek` as a variant."}]},{"title":"Practice words","body":"These are useful readings, not a ban on the accepted alternatives above.","list":["`Aen` → ah-ehn","`Azan` → ah-zahn","`Pelagae` → peh-lah-gah-eh","`Shaleth` → shah-leth","`Belshara` → bel-shah-rah","`Morlathar` → mor-lah-thar"]}]

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan counts, scales numbers, and handles simple arithmetic.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording:
Celan starts with a base set of number words, then builds upward with prefixes for tens, hundreds, thousands, and beyond.
Addition is usually shown by additive number building, while subtraction uses the marker Ven between number forms.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
Base numbers: Verin (0), Unar (1), Del (2), Tren (3), Quen (4), Peth (5), Senar (6), Sethe (7), Oven (8), Nevar (9), Tenar (10)
Tens: Ten-del = 20
Mixed number: Tenar unar = 11
Hundreds: Hek-unar = 100
Thousands: Mel-unar = 1,000
Ten-thousands: Fen-unar = 10,000
Hundred-thousands: Hek-Mel-unar = 100,000
Addition: Hek-quen Ten-peth = 450 (400 + 50)
Subtraction: Hek-quen Ven Hek-del = 400 - 200 = 200

grammar_guide.csv.rule_name: The Architecture of Relation: Prepositions, Place, and Time
grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan uses prepositions as the structural joints of relation, place, and time.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording:
Because Celan relies on a strict Verb-Subject-Object flow, prepositions do immense structural work.
They act as the architectural joints of a sentence, defining movement, accompaniment, absence, elevation, location, and temporal setting.
grammar_guide.csv.guideSections: [{"title":"The Structural Role of Prepositions","body":"In Celan, prepositions do an immense amount of structural work. Because the language relies on a strict Verb-Subject-Object flow, these small forms act as the architectural joints of a sentence, defining the precise nature of movement, accompaniment, absence, and elevation."},{"title":"The Core Relational Prepositions","body":"These are the primary markers a new learner should recognize first to navigate the world.","list":[{"title":"var","copy":"to, towards — direction or movement toward a destination."},{"title":"ser","copy":"with — accompaniment or shared presence."},{"title":"thal","copy":"from, out of — origin, or movement away from a source."},{"title":"ka","copy":"without — absence, lack, or separation from something."},{"title":"esh","copy":"above, over — elevation or superior positioning."},{"title":"morl","copy":"under, beneath — positioned below or physically grounded."}]},{"title":"Place and time","body":"`an` commonly introduces a place and also appears in established “in” expressions for time. `nor` explicitly introduces a time or period. Choose the form that expresses the intended relationship; `an kinnmor` (“in the morning”) is valid Celan.","list":[{"title":"an","copy":"at, in, or on; usually place, and also used in attested time expressions such as `an kinnmor` (in the morning)."},{"title":"nor","copy":"at, during, or in a time period; makes the time setting explicit."}]},{"title":"Canonical examples","body":null,"list":["var dren. — To the water.","var I ser ser. — I go with a friend.","tha-var la thal Terra. — They went from the Earth.","var I ka shal. — I go without light.","moraen I an Varthas. — I stand at the city.","nor-var I nor Kinnmor. — I will go in the morning.","weksharaen I an kinnmor. — I commute in the morning.","var I esh dren. — I go above the water.","var I morl dren. — I go beneath the water."]},{"title":"What to notice","body":"`an` and `nor` can both appear in sentences about time. `nor` marks the time setting explicitly; established phrases with `an` remain valid."}]

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan asks, negates a question, and gives a command.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording:
Start ordinary questions with ra.
For a negative question, place Ver before the verb.
For a direct command, start the sentence with va.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:

ra ver var ser an dren? — "Does the friend not go to the water?"
va var an dren! — "Go to the water!"

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How this part of Celan is meant to work.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: Celan verbs do not conjugate based on tense. Instead, tenses are indicated by prefixes and suffixes.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
Present: var I dren. / I go to the water.
Past: tha-var I dren. / I went to the water.
Future: nor-var I dren. / I will go to the water.
Continuous: varal I dren. / I am going to the water.
Perfective: varath I dren. / I have gone to the water.
Habitual: varas I dren. / I usually go to the water.
Also attested with explicit destination: var I an dren. The bare goal is attested for var; do not generalize it to every motion verb.

grammar_guide.csv.original_wording:
Negation is formed by placing Ver before the verb or noun.
● Verb Negation: Ver before the verb negates it.
● Noun Negation: Ver before a noun negates its existence.

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan turns one thing into many.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording:
Rule:
● -in is added to nouns ending in consonants.
● -n is added to nouns ending in vowels.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
● Ser (friend) → Serin (friends)
● Thar (heart) → Tharin (hearts)
● Esh (sky) → Eshin (skies)
● Dren (water) → Drenin (waters)
● Tera (home) → Teran (homes)

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How respect and social distance change phrasing.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording:
1. Casual/Familiar:
○ Use plain pronouns and address by name or role without modifiers.
2. Respectful/Polite:
○ Add Li- prefix to show respect.
3. Honorific/Formal-High Respect:
○ Use both Li- and -en suffix.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
var I dren, Ser. — I go to the water, friend.
var I dren, Li-Ser. — I go to the water, respected friend.
var Li-Ya dren. — You, respected one, go to the water.

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan asks, commands, and pushes a sentence forward.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: Standard questions begin with ra. In a content question a speaker may close the clause with mu what nu when zhe why sha how lo where or ri who to name the missing answer category. The closing particle is grammatically correct but optional. Without it context may supply the intended answer type. Ri does not distinguish English who from whom.
grammar_guide.csv.examples: ra var ser? / Where does the friend go? Context supplies place. / ra var ser lo? / Where does the friend go? Lo makes place explicit.
grammar_guide.csv.notes: User-approved canon expansion. Preserves the shorter source construction while adding an optional explicit frame.

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How ownership and belonging are marked.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: Standalone ka is exclusively without or no. Possessive -ka must be hyphenated to the possessor. Body parts, inner states, personal clothes, and primary personal gear use post-nominal -ian (my), -ya (your), or -oshen (his/her/their). Collective, titled, compound, and other third-person possessors use possessor-ka. La-ka kelvor (“their mouth”) is also an established third-person body-part construction. -ian never means their. Relational -esh indicates a bond; it does not by itself specify a third-person owner.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
I-ka dren — My water.
Ilin-ka emil — Our meal.
rinaen aiv an doran-ian. — There is pain in my torso.
drenselaen I noka-ian. — I wash my vulva.
La-ka kelvor — Their mouth.
Var I ka shal. — I go without light.
grammar_guide.csv.notes: ED-0037 / ED-0038: user-approved review and subsequent possession clarification.

grammar_guide.csv.rule_name: Two permitted orders for a governing verb and its complement
grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How this sentence pattern is meant to work.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: Both V1 + Subject + V2 + Object and V1 + V2 + Subject + Object are permitted. The first places the subject directly after the governing verb; the second presents the combined action before the subject.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
siv I pralaen krezor. — I try to make the hearth.
siv gavaen I zor. — I try to hunt the animal.
sivrethaen belnoraen rakumek nor mekreth. — The computers fail to synchronize during the system malfunction.
grammar_guide.csv.notes: ED-0037 / ED-0038: user-approved review and subsequent possession clarification.

grammar_guide.csv.rule_name: Varan and the universal continuous suffix
grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How this part of Celan is meant to work.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: `-al` marks continuous action. `Varan` is a separate, established word built from Var + An; it means to reside, stay, or be located at a physical place. It does not make `-an` a general continuous ending. `an` commonly marks place and also occurs in established time expressions such as `an kinnmor`; `nor` explicitly marks time.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
varal I dren. — I am going to the water.
varan I an Varthas. — I am residing in the city.
nor-var I an Varthas. — I will go to the city.
grammar_guide.csv.notes: ED-0037 / ED-0038: user-approved review and subsequent possession clarification.
grammar_guide.csv.source_section: User-approved grammar decisions
grammar_guide.csv.preview: -al remains the universal continuous suffix.

gr-dr1-0003 varan and the universal continuous suffix aspect and location grammar tools user-approved grammar decisions -al remains the universal continuous suffix. varan is the lexicalized locative-stative form var + an: to reside, stay, or be located at a physical place. it does not establish continuous -an. an supplies physical location; nor supplies time. varal i dren. — i am going to the water.
varan i an varthas. — i am residing in the city.

grammar_guide.csv.purpose: How Celan turns one thing into many.
grammar_guide.csv.original_wording: The existing plural rule remains: consonant-final nouns take -in; vowel-final nouns take -n. Separately, -in has an approved person/participant sense connecting a person or group to a bond, place, or category. That sense does not replace ordinary plurals.
grammar_guide.csv.examples:
nderun — testicles.
welrinin — citizens.
Shalor-in — one belonging to the sanctuary.
grammar_guide.csv.notes: ED-0037 / ED-0038: user-approved review and subsequent possession clarification.
